utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ladies and gentlemen, good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-84-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I have the appearances. Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to my learned friends. I'm Patricia Sellers from the office of the Prosecution. And with me today are my co-counsel Mr. Gilles Dutertre, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Mr. Anees Ahmed, and Ms. Nicole Rizer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers. For the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Ben Emmerson, and I am counsel for Mr. Haradinaj, and I appear together with my co-counsel Mr. Rodney Dixon, assisted by Marina Aksenova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning. Gregor Guy-Smith appearing on behalf of Ibriz Balaj and assisted by Bart Willemsen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Richard Harvey appearing on behalf of Lahi Brahimaj. Together with me are Mr. Paul Troop, my co-counsel, and assisted by Antonietta Trapani, who is our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Before going on further, I'd like to make sure that the accused are following in a language they understand. However, I take it that Mr. Haradinaj is not present, being on provisional release.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Balaj. THE ACCUSED BALAJ: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you following this procedure in the language you understand? THE ACCUSED BALAJ: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about Mr. Brahimaj? THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. My understanding is that this is the fifth Status Conference but, however, it is my first Status Conference after the change in the composition of the Chamber in last July. Due to the unavailability of the -- certain Defence counsel for a so-called 65 ter Conference, my understanding is the Senior Legal Officer requested the parties to put in writing the items they wished to discuss at this Status Conference, and I was able to briefly go through that item, and I have to say that I'm very much benefited from the submissions. I have one suggestion that I would like -- if the parties do not object, I would like the Defence submission, three of them, to be filed officially so that we don't have to go through each item in detail, without having to go through -- into items in detail. We can refer to them in the courtroom. Would it be okay with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Certainly. That would be a perfectly convenient way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Having said that, then I will follow the items noted by Mr. Emmerson in Haradinaj's Defence submission basically. So therefore I would like to deal with the pending motions first of all, but I take it that parties should have received the two decisions I've issued yesterday. Can I confirm that? I see nodding all from the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has received the protective motion decision. We have not received the other decision at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both decisions are related to protective measures, but other thing I take it that it is a decision on the protective measures for certain forensic documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we thank you that that decision has come out. No, we have not received it. I have been informed by our case manager that she has just -- has received an electronic copy. So we're unaware at this point in time of its contents, but we appreciate the decisions having been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should make clear that the Defence is in the same position. The nods that Your Honour observed were nods of confirmation that we, too, had yesterday received the decision in relation to Witness 756, but the other decision has not or certainly hadn't found its way to us at the time of final preparation for this morning's hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. This is a confidential decision, so I'd better not deal with it in open session. Yes. Then I will come to the outstanding motions, which are of -- there are four items in number. The first and the most important thing is the amendment of indictment, and -- which is outstanding for some time, and the Chamber is of the view it is urgent to deal with this matter, and we're going to give some priority to this motion. And I think I can say without -- well, speaking for myself, the Chamber would be able to dispose of the decision by -- before the end of this month. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you again for recognising me. Since Your Honour has already approached the issue of amendment of indictment, in particular with the outstanding motion, the Prosecution would like to just intercede and we can take our time later on in the hearing if you so deem, but to say that we would be informing the Trial Chamber at this time point in the session that we will be coming forward with another motion to amend. This is in view of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. You are saying that you would propose to amend the indictment once again?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. We were going to address this to Your Honour a bit later on in the session. I'm only bringing it up now because that might in some ways modify the need to have to put out a decision concerning the amendments that we proposed before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it related to the item in your 65 ter letter named as alteration of the Lake Radonjic crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It is not related to that. It's related to the last item that we put on the agenda today. The Prosecution informed both the Defence and the Trial Chamber that we would be seeking further amendment to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell me briefly the skeleton of the proposed amendment, briefly?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We propose, within the contents of the Trial Chamber or the former Pre-Trial Judge having already raised the issue of Rule 73 bis, to streamline the indictment. In this manner, we would like to, as a matter of fact, remove some of the currently alleged criminal conduct, and we intend to drop some of the counts, and we would like to put the indictment in a format which would be easier both for the Prosecution to proceed with its case, but we also think it would make it clearer in terms of due process rights of the accused and of the Trial Chamber that would be presiding over the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Sellers. Without having to hear from the Defence, that gesture or that step of the Prosecution should be welcome very much, and I wonder if there should be any addition of charges.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point in time the additional charges would only relate to those that are currently before the trial bench in terms of the amendment, or the move to amend the indictment that have been held earlier, in May. Other than that, Your Honour, we do not seek additional charges. We'd like to incorporate that amendment now within our next amendment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your suggestion would not affect at all the disposition of current motion which is pending before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would affect it only to extent, if you would prefer, to hold in abeyance your decision on the current amendment, and we will incorporate that evidence that is before you for the current amendment in this new motion to seek leave to amend the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in order to have a complete -- complete indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sort of.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having heard that, we can dispose of the current motion, ordering the Prosecution to produce a new -- I'm not sure whether it should be granted or not. We can order the Prosecution to produce a final indictment in a very not lengthy time. Can I say so?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I think that you can say that. And I think that we would also proprio motu from the Prosecution would like to file an amended indictment within a short delay of time, and we envision that that filing should be certainly within two weeks and we really anticipate for it to be sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But without having to wait for our decision on the amendment of the indictment, could you not file that amendment as -- another amendment as soon as possible, say, next week?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we would attempt to file it toward the end of next week, but because of certain issues that are still currently being discussed, it might be at the beginning of the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That's still before the end of this month. Then --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then Trial Chamber will be in the position to deal with it comprehensively.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That would be our intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think there would be any opposition in relation to that from the Defence. Any observation? Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: My only observations are these: We had notice of this just a few moments before coming to this morning's hearing and obviously have only those details which Ms. Sellers has sketched out to Your Honour this morning. Plainly we welcome the abandonment of criminal charges. We welcome the reduction in the scope of criminal allegations on the indictment. Insofar as the Prosecution propose to persist, however, with the application to amend by an addition of a count on the indictment, which is reflected in the existing motion that's presently pending before the Trial Chamber, we wonder whether in fact given the length of time that that motion has been outstanding the more appropriate course would not be for the Trial Chamber to proceed to rule on that motion given that it is, as Your Honour has observed, entirely independent of the Prosecution's proposed reduction in the scope of the charges that currently sit on the indictment. Plainly, at the end a compendious indictment will need to be filed, but there is a substantive decision to be made on the addition of the count, which is already the subject of a closed exchange of pleadings. The concern, obviously, that we have is that there has been already some considerable delay in that respect for reasons that of course all parties well understand, but we are anxious that further delay which could be avoided is avoided, and in those circumstances we would certainly invite you to consider whether the appropriate course is not to rule on the existing motion, and as Your Honour has suggested, for the Prosecution to file the motion insofar as it relates to the reduction in the scope of the existing criminal allegations, and that can be dealt with either at the same time or very shortly afterwards. And insofar as the skeleton that Ms. Sellers has provided is concerned, we understand what she has said to be an indication that there will be no expansion of the Prosecution's allegations in relation to the modes of criminal participation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll bear that in mind. And I encourage the Prosecution to file another amendment as soon as possible. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to clarify one thing and it might be just the terminology of my learned friend. We will not be expanding in terms of the numbers of counts; we will be substituting some counts for others. But I believe that my learned friend just mentioned the modes of responsibility, and I did not say that we would not be expanding the modes of liability. I talked about the criminal conduct and the counts. Just to make sure that that was clear on the record. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Ms. Sellers. You said substituting count?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Meaning substituting something that we find that might be legally characterised under a provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not new facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Not new facts, Your Honour. And that's what I'd like to emphasise. We're not talking about additional facts or conduct other than what is before Your Honour right now. We're talking about a refinement of the indictment in terms of legal characterisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. We will see what will come out. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the comments just made by Ms. Sellers, it seems that the suggestion made by Mr. Emmerson then may well be -- I would adopt that suggestion, that the Chamber at this point make a determination on the pending motion. If I'm not mistaken, what I believe I just heard is we are potentially looking at different modes of liability being pled in the new application. If that be the case, then why don't we say that now so we understand that, because I think it would be of assistance to the Chamber in making a determination of what would procedurally be the better way of proceeding at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you elaborate a bit more on the -- [Albanian on English channel]. I think the English channel has been interrupted. It seems to be okay now. Could you elaborate on the substituting mode of liability a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And for sake of clarity as a matter of fact, I believe that learned counsel does understand. The Prosecution will allege, and allege based upon the same conduct other modes of liability. And that's why I wanted to no mislead our learned friend who made the comment relating to modes of liability. I spoke about substitution of charges, and that is unrelated to what I've just informed the Trial Chamber and Defence of modes of liability. That is related to the legal characterisation of certain counts. In reviewing our evidence, we believe that certain counts might be characterised better under another legal provision. It will not increase the number of counts. It will refine the indictment so that the accused understand and have a clearer ability to defend themselves against the criminal conduct that the Prosecution has already placed within its indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think I understand in full.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I give you an example, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's substituting 7(1) to 7(3)?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm speaking about, on the one hand, and very clearly to say that these are oral submissions and that we were going to detail them in written submissions, but just for sake of clarification. For example, substituting counts that at this point in time might allege cruel treatment if we find that that evidence is sufficient not only for cruel treatment but for a count of torture, we will then substitute, no longer proceed on a count of cruel treatment and might choose to proceed on a count of torture. If we find that the conduct of the accused lends itself not only to joint criminal enterprise but to another form of individual criminal responsibility, we might in the alternative plead that form. Not increasing the number of counts but correctly, more correctly, characterising the conduct of the accused and the liability that the accused is thus exposed to and the liability that they must defend themselves with. Your Honour, if I haven't made myself clear, please, I'm open for your suggestions on how to refine the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At this time, I don't think it's beneficial for both parties and for the Chamber as well to go further without having looked at the actual proposal for the amendment or the substituting charges. So after the motion will have been filed, the Chamber will consider what step of action will be most appropriate and decide whether to decide the current pending motion alone or two motions altogether. Any suggestions from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I had, if I may, two short observations. I see the force in the suggestion that the Prosecution's draft amended indictment should be filed before the Trial Chamber rules on the pending motion so that the two can be side by side before the Trial Chamber, although I don't at the moment see it as being necessary for the existing motion to be either dismissed or withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But given that the current motion was hoped at least to have been decided by the end of this month, then we would request that the Prosecution be given a very clear direction that the timetable that they are proposing for the filing of the amended indictment by the end of next week be strictly adhered to so that the Trial Chamber is in a position to render its decision on the existing motion which, as Your Honour's recognised, is one requiring expediency without any further delay. The other observation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but the Prosecution did not say the end of next week but sometime week after. So given the 24th, Tuesday, is a holiday, UN holiday, I would like to suggest the Prosecution would file its proposed motion by 25th, Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. The Prosecution will following that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And Your Honour, the second point. May I thank Ms. Sellers for the clarification and to record again arising out of the exchange that has occurred that it is our understanding then that an allegation under 7(3) is not proposed as part of the new amendments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And related to that amendment of indictment is the deadline to file pre-trial briefs from the Prosecution and the Defence as well, so at this moment I'd like to suggest that the deadline currently set is not valid, which is obvious, and when the Chamber will issue the decision on the amendment of indictment I shall, or the Chamber will, at the same time will give the guideline or set the deadline to file the pre-trial briefs respectively. The previous -- previous deadline for the Defence was set two weeks after the Prosecution's filing of pre-trial briefs, but my impression from the top of my head is rather some are short, so I have in mind about a month from the Prosecution's filing. Would it be okay with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, particularly in light of the suggestion that the indictment may look different in shape to the indictment that is currently before the parties, a period of four weeks would be certainly valuable from the point of the view of the Defence of Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. I take it that Mr. Guy-Smith and Mr. Harvey take also the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I concur. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So do I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, motion, second one, which Chamber find also urgent and important is a protective -- is motion concerning the lifting redactions of witness statement filed by the Defence. The Chamber will also give priority to this motion in dealing with several pre-trial cases pending before the Trial Chamber. However, I wonder whether parties can reach a kind of compromise. Can we briefly go into a private session, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, as soon as practicable, could you file in writing whether Prosecution is opposed to the disclosure of those materials we referred to to the named Defence counsels' legal assistants. Or are you in a position to answer the question right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do not oppose any such thing. We do not oppose that assistants have access to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't seek to complicate this matter further, but as has already been mentioned, up until recently Mr. Guy-Smith and I both shared the services of Mr. Willemsen as our case manager. He is now working exclusively for the Balaj team, and Ms. Trapani is now my case manager and legal assistant for these purposes, and so I would ask that she also be granted the same access as given to Ms. Parker and Mr. Willemsen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I have the name again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Antonietta Trapani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have it. Yes, Ms. Trapani. Do you have any observation, Mr. Dutertre?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's go back to my original question, whether we can reach a similar compromise in relation to the motion by the Defence lifting the redaction of the witness statements. So how about disclosing unredacted, full statements to the Defence counsel but not the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without -- I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I would just like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm just asking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly. And we certainly want to promote a spirit of cooperation. The Prosecution must, however, place on the record and inform Your Honour that our concern relates to witness protection and witness security issues, and that if Your Honour were to suggest that at this point that the redactions and the identity and identifying whereabouts be lifted, we're obliged to speak to our witnesses and inform them of this. And, Your Honour, at that point I believe that the danger that they might be exposed to could increase, and their fear and anticipation prior to that 30-day time period would be affected. But in a spirit of cooperation, I think that what we can do is inform the Defence and Your Honours that we will look again as we are refining our witness list to see if there are any persons who are now no longer affected by the Defence request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have asked this question, because at any rate, Prosecution is due to disclose those material 30 days before the commencement of trial, which is roughly saying early next year, say February or March, and then -- a month before that is January. So it's not far from here -- from now. So there's no big deal disclosing only to the Defence counsel and specific legal assistants at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate your observations, and I think based upon our response to the Defence motion we understand that the Defence would not be able to disclose only to Defence counsel. They would, of course, during the course of investigations expose the names, identifying whereabouts to investigators, possibly to their own witnesses in inquiries about certain persons, and other third parties, and I believe that's the rationale behind the 30-day disclosure. I know that we are approaching that deadline, and we believe, and I think the Trial Chamber prior to this, and other Trial Chambers within the Tribunal, have seen the 30-day period to be a adequate period of time for the witnesses who will be called at trial. The Prosecution would just like to renew its stance on the open record and to say again that we would like to cooperate possibly by refining the people that are affected by this Defence motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it that you are opposing to that idea, but -- so that being the case, the Chamber will deal with the motion as promptly as possible. Any observation, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make three short observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: First of all, on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj, we have always adopted a strategy in our dealings with the Prosecution and with the Trial Chamber in relation to protective measures, whereby we would not make applications for the lifting of protective measures unless or until a point had been reached in our investigations when we needed to have redactions lifted in order effectively to prepare for trial. And so that, for example, at the outset of these proceedings we did not oppose protective measures because we felt the appropriate course was to apply to have them limited on a case-by-case basis once it became clear that the redactions were obstructing effective Defence preparation. And on reviewing the file, Your Honour will see that we made our first group of applications in relation to a series of witnesses, all of whom gave evidence about or in relation to allegations concerning the Jablanica area. All of the arguments that Ms. Sellers has raised today and have -- the Prosecution have raised in their written motion were made in relation to those series of witnesses, and the former Trial Chamber's view, rather like the observation that you have just expressed, was that with each of these witnesses it is not a question of whether this information is going to be disclosed but when, and the when being an issue which is relevant to the most effective Defence preparation. And as I've indicated, we proceeded on a case-by-case basis, and we have reached a point at which that material is necessary for the purposes of completing our investigations prior to trial. There's quite a lot of redacted material in there, and 30 days prior to trial places an unnecessary constraint, given that inevitably that material will in due course and in a relatively short period be disclosed to the Defence in any event. Which leads me on to the second point. There is a difference between forensics disclosure and the redactions which are sought to be lifted by this motion. Forensics disclosure where redacted material was in issue went to Defence counsel and to the experts because it was only relevant to expert analysis. None of the information that was redacted was information which had the substantive relevance to the investigation of counts. It was, for example, identifying material for the donors of DNA samples who are not witnesses necessarily in the case but had simply donated their DNA for the purposes of comparison. Ms. Sellers is quite right to anticipate the Defence's response to Your Honour's this suggestion. The purpose of having these redactions lifted, as our motions make clear, is a measured and as we submit a proportionate way to advance the Defence investigation. So whilst of course identifications could remain confidential for the purposes of the general public or third parties, we most certainly want to be able to disclose the identifications that are lifted to our investigators. And finally, we again welcome the indication from Ms. Sellers that the Prosecution will review the necessity for the maintenance of protective measures in respect of those witnesses themselves. That is a duty of review that we would imagine was an ongoing one and that the Prosecution would in any event be conducting on a continuous basis, even after protective measures have been authorised where they think they have no longer got good grounds to maintain them, but it's not as we would submit a reason in any way to delay the ruling that the motions now require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll bear that in mind in dealing with the motion. While I encourage very much the voluntary cooperation between the parties, but the Chamber -- as for Chambers as well, we'll do our best to determine the issue as soon as possible. Third one -- the third outstanding motion is a -- one related to the protective measures for Witness SST7/38. But in the meantime, can I ask what the abbreviation of SST7 means at all? It's a very odd form of pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, SST7 that you find before the number of the witness relates, I believe, but I might stand corrected, I think it's related to team 7. That's the number of the team that is in charge of the case, the name of the investigator's team. Then you have and slash, and then the number of the witness 38, 29, whatever. That's the number of the protected witness. So we will move from SST7/1 to SST7/X, depending on the number given to each particular witness. That's the explanation I can give you on that. And as far as this particular witness is concerned, we are talking about someone who's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I know who this witness is about. This is related to the added part of the amended indictment proposal. Yes. And the -- my understanding is that the -- this decision is delayed or postponed until the determination of the -- whether -- as to whether to grant the amendment or not. However, it was my practice as a Pre-Trial Judge, or the practice of the Trial Chamber I formerly belonged to, was somewhat different, i.e., we allowed those materials to be disclosed to the Defence, i.e. -- to put it otherwise, the supporting material upon which the proposed amendment of the indictment or new charges were based upon should be disclosed. It is because the Chamber should hear from the Defence, and the Chamber would be benefitted from the Defence submission, although once the indictment is confirmed or leave has been granted, it is not for the Defence to challenge the -- such confirmation or amendment on the ground that there's no prima facie case. So I'm minded, inclined, if the Defence so wishes and there is no serious objection from the Prosecution, to order the Prosecutor to disclose those statements with any redaction the Prosecution deems necessary on a provisional or temporary basis until the Chamber's final decision after the determination of the indictment issue. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would not oppose that suggestion as long as it is understood that any redactions, removing of identity is done for the ease of the Defence to be able to look at the documents, and it's not in any manner the Prosecution trying to obviate a Trial Chamber order while the issue is still before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it there would be no objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: On the contrary. It was the position that we advocated prior to the decision of your predecessor, namely that we ought to see the material so that we could make submissions, and at that stage the position of the Prosecution was in opposition and we're grateful that that position has changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it is so ordered. That as soon as practicable the Prosecution will disclose those statements to the Defence with the redactions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to make that clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On a provisional basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. That is the distinguishing points between our prior argument and what learned counsel is submitting now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the object of that strategy is that the Defence might have an opportunity to make any comments that would assist the Trial Chamber in determining the application to amend and given the timetable which is currently proposed for the application itself, may we therefore invite you to direct the Prosecution to disclose that document to us forthwith, that is to say, within the next 48 hours at the outside, and then we may have an opportunity to file any submissions arising out of it in sufficient time for them to be with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Forty-eight hours from now is sometime on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, two working days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will it suit the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we will do it forthwith. I must be quite frank. I did not believe my learned friend will have it on Sunday afternoon, but certainly we will move on that. And I think that with the understanding, too, that we certainly don't mind giving courtesy copies in order to have it disclosed as soon as possible, but we would like to make sure that it stays within the parameters that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: -- Your Honour has set forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like to believe in voluntary -- the spirit of cooperation of the Prosecution, and if the Defence does not receive that statement until sometime Tuesday or Wednesday, the Defence can come up with a motion to the Pre-Trial Judge. The last outstanding motion, as I understand it, is the -- which was filed yesterday, and I -- which I saw just part of it without annexes is related to the access of a note of a witness. Mr. Dutertre, propose to going into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to come back to our previous point. I believe that if we look at the situation and the nature of the witness we've just discussed, if the Defence was to make its submission on a confidential basis, that would be very appropriate. And if the amendment of the indictment is not granted, then thus we would avoid making public all sorts of information related to a witness would not testify. That I wanted to add and I believe that the Defence will not object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it for granted to the Defence should have understood it. Yes. Witness 29. Having read the submission from the Defence, and I have no knowledge in detail about that, but are you in the position to respond to that motion right now or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were alerted to the motion when the Defence counsel put forward their issues for today's Status Conference, and then we received the motion yesterday, early evening. We have had a chance to read the motion. We would like to preserve our right to respond within the 14 days. And we had put it on our list also just to say that we would be able to inform the Trial Chamber, not what position we would take but what procedural position we would take, and we would rest behind your rights to reply within a 14-day period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I will turn to the issue of disclosure. The first thing mentioned in the submission is for disclosure of forensic materials. Is this matter to be resolved by one of the decisions I've issued yesterday, or it refers to different forensic materials? Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It may be that in due course Mr. Dutertre will be in a better position to answer that question in full, but our understanding is that the list that appears on page 3, the bullet-point list that appears on page 3 of our memorandum includes a series of items that are not amongst the redacted material, which is the subject of the decision that Your Honour made yesterday. We've set out the history in very short order, and without at this stage rehearsing all of the details or treading over old ground between the parties, the short fact is that a series of deadlines has come and passed by which the Prosecution have promised and been required to serve material in their forensic case, and we are still in the position that quite apart from the redacted confidential material there are significant areas of material that have not yet been served in a case which has some not inconsiderable forensic complexities. And Your Honour will see, for example, in the first bullet point that there is a substantial body of DNA identification material which is still outstanding in respect of quite a large number of sets of remains. That is material which is obviously extremely important from the Defence point of view, as is each of the other items. The fourth bullet point, for example, was a -- or is a requested witness statement from the investigator Barney Kelly who has had overall responsibility for the forensic side of the investigation in what, as I say, is a complex case with a series of exhumations and continuity and identification problems. And that is a statement that has been the subject of discussion for more than six months and has been promised on a large number of occasions but is still not forthcoming. Forensic disclosure has been a blight in this case, and the unfortunate consequence of the motion that was filed seeking a further order on redactions appears to have been that the Prosecution has suspended, or partially suspended full disclosure of the forensic material that was otherwise in their possession, and indeed we're told that there were some 2.000 or so pages of material to be served upon us but which it has been held back pending the outcome of a motion on which, as far as we are able at this stage to see, it does not depend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Dutertre, the items mentioned in the Defence submission, in particular Mr. Emmerson's submission, are those not the items that Prosecution pledged to make available by the end of June this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for the schedule of disclosure, many things have happened. Many discussions have taken place. It would be difficult to summarise all this in a few words. We don't have enough time. What is sure is that the Prosecution has disclosed everything it received, and what we didn't have we could not disclose to the Defence. What was put on standby was what we received following our motion for protective measures dated 25th of August, 2006, the motion you ruled upon yesterday. But everything else was disclosed to the Defence. In the letter of the 6th of June, 2006, I listed a number of material that should be disclosed and that were disclosed. I also mentioned a number of investigations for which I was not able to state when I would receive the relevant documents, and we have to remember that the Prosecution depends on other organisations for this matter, and we have to wait, and we have to wait the outcome of the work of these organisations in order to get the relevant information. In a way, the Prosecution is in the same position as the Defence. We are waiting for documents as eagerly as the Defence. So as far as receiving and disclosing forensic material, we are on an equal footing, the Defence and the Prosecution. At page 3 of the Defence submissions dated the 11th of October, 2006, we find a number of issues, a number of questions, and you've answered a number of them with your decision. But as early as next week we'll disclose the rest of the documents, 2.000 pages, plus all the documents we've received since then. A number of documents that are listed there are not here. We do not have. If you think it useful, I could provide additional information to the Defence if you believe that it would be useful for the preparation of the Defence. It might be rather long, but I could do it if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't wish to be too long. I shall proceed with each item, one after the other. I should like to start off with the genetic reports. All the genetic reports that have been prepared by the International Commission for Missing Persons have been disclosed over the last few months. We have a number of documents that list those documents that have already been disclosed. We can hand them round right now, and we can clearly identify at which time and which moment these documents have been disclosed. When I say that these documents, I'm talking about the genetic documents, both negative and positive alike. There is some positive genetic material which hasn't been made available to us yet. We hope to be getting this in the next two weeks. This really -- this refers to RR -- RRE21003BP as well as body ACM for the exhumation which took place in 2005. As soon as I get these genetic reports, it will be disclosed to the Defence. As far as the unidentified bodies are concerned, I am afraid, and I can only regret this, that these bodies remain unidentified, and therefore we have no genetic reports for the latter. And the two reports which I have just mentioned should complete the list of identified persons. So much for the genetic reports. Perhaps the Defence would like to put questions to me on this matter before I proceed and I could then answer their questions straight away rather than answering all the questions at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So briefly the list of disclosed documents, already disclosed documents. Yes. Just a second. Sorry. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may, as Mr. Dutertre has just indicated, respond by saying as he has correctly pointed out there are two sets of remains. There are those that are identified and named as such in the indictment; and then there are those that are unidentified and unnamed. There are certain, as Mr. Dutertre has indicated, reports still being awaited for those persons who have been identified; I think it's in the region of about four or five. And it would be good if we could get a confirmation of exactly how many reports are awaited and also by when those should arrive. We were at the last Status Conference, if I may say so, in exactly the same position where Mr. Dutertre was saying that these reports are awaited, there's very little they can do to obtain them and that it's a matter that's out of their hands. And we're now in a position where, once again, we're still waiting for those reports, and it's got to a point where steps do need to be taken to ensure that those organisations are followed up by the OTP as quickly as possible to obtain those reports. So that's the first part of it. The second part, it relates to those remains that are unidentified, and they -- in a recent letter sent by the OTP on the 27th of September it was indicated -- and it's approximately 12 of those are still being be examined where DNA reports are awaited. It was the OTP saying that those reports are awaited. And once again, the question should be when do we expect to receive those reports and what steps have been taken to obtain them as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Perhaps once again I'm confused because this is a drum that I've been beating for a long period of time. When the term is used, "DNA reports," I take it what Mr. Dutertre means are conclusions without the underlying information forms the basis of that conclusion. If in fact that is what he means by a report, the Defence has yet to receive that underlying data which forms the basis of the conclusion contained, and to that extent we do not have that information. And this is information that has been under discussion now for close to 10 months, more specifically under discussion for quite a number of months as a result of specific requests by letter sent to the OTP with regard to the underlying information that forms the basis of the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dutertre, are you in the position to address those three issues -- or two issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As far as the genetic reports are concerned, I still expect to receive two positive genetic reports. I know according to the information I have that these reports have been prepared, and I await these to be handed over to me by Minuk. I hope -- by UNMIK. I hope that I will be receiving these in the next two weeks. As far as unidentified bodies are concerned, I regret that these remain identified bodies, and for the sake of the families I regret it, of course. Also, we have looked at genetic profiles, at bone analysis, and there seems to be no direct correlation between blood samples of the families. I can't say any more about this. I think we can reasonably say that no further identification, unless something unexpected occurs, will occur. So these are the two -- these are the reports which will be disclosed over the next two weeks. As far as what Mr. Guy-Smith said, in fact these are the conclusions of the definitive reports. These include the names of the relatives of the victim, the name of the identified victim, and genetic sequences which I've explained in the past. I explained that these were encoded because ICMP, the International Commission for Missing People, wish to protect these people. So as far as these reports are concerned, admittedly we have provided the conclusions. However, there are annexes to our 25th of August, 2006, motion. These annexes will be disclosed as soon as next week do -- for a number of victims do meet the requirements of Mr. Guy-Smith. This has to do with the case file of genetic analysis which was sent and which is a very comprehensive file which was sent by the International Commission for Missing Persons. So I'm talking now about cases in which the families have authorised this, because there is a certain amount of personal and confidential data contained in these. When the families could not be contacted or would not grant authorisation for the comprehensive genetic analysis to be provided, then it is the definitive and -- report which has been given to the Defence. For a number of victims the data will be provided as far as next -- as soon as next week. I hope I have answered the questions put by Mr. Guy-Smith and other Defence counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any further reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was most helpful, but there's still a matter outstanding, and that relates to the remains which are not identified in any form at this point, and Mr. Dutertre says that they remain unidentified, and that's the end of the story. However, and this is the clarification that I seek, is that the Prosecution's letter that I referred to on the 27th of September mentions that a number of DNA reports are awaited from the OMPF.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which mentions 12 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, and Mr. Dutertre has now said that two further reports are coming. My question is what about the other reports that the OTP have said they are waiting for. When are those due to arrive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult to answer this question. If we'd had a positive report between -- in the database, if we were able to establish a correlation between the blood samples and the bone samples, we would then be expecting further reports, but to date I only expect to receive the two reports which I've just mentioned. Once again, I regret this, but the other bodies will probably not be identified unless something unexpected occurs. So that's all I can say concerning this matter. The group of identified persons, after the two reports I've mentioned will be disclosed, should be complete, and I don't think we should expect any further identification unless something quite unexpected occurs. If that's the case, well, that would be the case, but I don't expect it. That's all I can say, Your Honour, about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I take it that you are supposing that there will be no further identification unless something quite unexpected occurs? Yeah, I think that's the farthest we can reach at this moment. Why don't we believe it there and move on to another topic, but I'd like to go back to the original issue of disclosing forensic matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I heard the -- it would be no problem for the Prosecution to disclose them by next week, so I would order the same time line, by the 25th, Wednesday, the week after. So I order the Prosecutor to disclose all the items mentioned in the Defence motion, and if there's anything they cannot disclose, provide the Chamber with the reasons why they cannot disclose those specific items.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour. We shall certainly disclose everything we have at our disposal which we've received recently, and we shall also disclose in detail all those documents which we -- which we shall receive in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So these -- I would like to make sure this access will be granted to the named three Defence counsels' assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All documents will be disclosed. That said, there are a number other issues which relate to our ongoing investigation, and these are items which we shall disclose in due course. But I was referring to all the genetic documents. I was not talking about witness testimonies here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And as for yesterday's ruling I made and having heard the Prosecution's submission, they have no objections. I'm minded to put a corrigendum to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to that, and I'm grateful for Your Honour's indication of a deadline, but I may just have one point clarified? Mr. Dutertre's response is that material in the Prosecution's possession will be disclosed, and of course he's made the point that material that the Prosecution has not received is not in their possession and they cannot disclose it, but if Your Honour were to cast an eye down to the fourth and fifth bullet points on item 3, the fourth is not a document that depends on any party outside the Office of the Prosecutor , it is a narrative witness statement explaining the forensic examination from the point of the Serbian analysis in 1998 right the way through until the DNA analyses that are taking place at the moment. It's -- what has been specified as a request is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I beg your point. Bullet points 4 and 5 on page?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The fourth and fifth on page 3 of our document, Your Honour, which would fall within Your Honour's ruling, are material that must be generated by the Prosecution itself. One is a full narrative explanation of the chronology of the forensic examinations and the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I was looking at a different document. Page 3, bullet points --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Page 3. Fourth bullet point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One of the investigator's statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Just so that it's clear, Your Honour will have seen that there have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you suggest that Prosecution should produce a statement from this investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We've suggested it for many months, it's been promised for many months. Because of the complexity of the forensic investigation -- and therefore that needs now to be the subject of a duty of disclosure and there's been no suggestion that it isn't coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which does not exist at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it exists or it doesn't, but if it doesn't it should. And if it doesn't, it must be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's deal with one by one. Yes, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As far as the testimonies are concerned, there are a number of short testimonies which I would like to talk about. These will be disclosed to the Defence as soon as they are completed and no later than the filing of the pre-trial brief, unless there are a few exceptional cases. As far as Barney Kelly is concerned, he looked after the exhumation that took place in 2005. I think the Defence would like him to discuss the entire genetic process and all the forensic aspects in this case. He was looking after the exhumation that took place in 2005. I'm still waiting for the genetic report to be provided for 2005. This is something I do not have yet. If Mr. Barney Kelly were to complete his statement, it would only be a partial statement and it would have to be completed thereafter. I think this will be completed -- this will be disclosed quickly, but I think I have to get the genetic report first before being able to provide a full answer. And I once mentioned that the deadline should be the same both for Mr. Barney Kelly and the report, in which case we will have Mr. Barney Kelly's statement without the report, and maybe it -- it will be provided to us afterwards. So this is my position so far. If Mr. Barney Kelly has not completed his statement, it's because new information has been coming in August and in September, and it was impossible to have an overall picture of what happened in 2005. So much for Mr. Barney Kelly's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: May I make a suggestion -- Mr. Guy-Smith, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, perhaps where the difficulty lies is that the Defence has been too eager in obtaining this information since we were informed on May 16th, the day before one of our 65 ter conferences, that this information would be compiled by the Prosecution and Mr. Kelly would be forwarding that information to us. It was matter that was discussed in the 65 ter on the 17th of May, and at that point we were informed that we would be receiving such a report. So perhaps the problem is that our notion of the passage of time is a bit different than that of the Prosecution. However, I think that at this point in time perhaps they should become a bit more in accord with our notion of time and get us the information, because as you indicated, we are fast approaching a trial date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is why I was about to make a suggestion to the Prosecution. So would it be plausible for the Prosecution to produce Mr. Kelly's statement to the extent he can say at the moment and put an addendum later on when he receives the remaining of the reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's quite -- it's quite possible, Your Honour, and we can agree with that. We can then file an addendum later on. That would not pose any problem. We could be in a position to provide something to the Defence very quickly. It's very possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then when do you think you can disclose Mr. Kelly's statement to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would need to get in touch with Mr. Kelly to answer this question. I know that he's currently on a mission, or he's going on a mission in the next few days so we are talking about not this week but the following. I'm not quite sure when he comes back from his mission, but I don't want to promise something I can't hold, so next week would not quite be possible but the week after that, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I would like to put a deadline for that by the end of this month. I think it would be safe. Unless there's any objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's perfectly all right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's done. The next issue, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next bullet point, it may well be subsumed within the new amended indictment, but may I just sketch it in and clarify that it is. We have been pressing for some time for the Prosecution to give us the details of the identifications of alleged victims who currently are listed on the indictment as unidentified remains but whom the Prosecution have indicated to us since the spring would be the subject of named particulars, though not necessarily new counts. Now, the Prosecution's position has been, and it's rather an opaque one to follow, but the Prosecution's position to date has been that they could not provide that information until the existing outstanding motion to amend the indictment, to add a new completely unrelated count had been determined, because it might affect the overall shape of a consistent new indictment. Providing it is clear that when the Prosecution files the proposed amended indictment in accordance with Your Honour's order, the particulars that we have been pressing for will then be finally included so that the Prosecution will identify in terms whose remains they say they are in a position evidentially to establish the identification of, then that will dispose of bullet point 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The question of what I've always called the update of the indictment, adding the name of victims, that will be part of what we mentioned at the beginning related to -- in relation with the indictment. Before filing a second amendment, a motion for a second amendment, we decided to wait for the decision about the first amendment, and we also decided to wait because we had not received the final genetic reports, and I've mentioned that I'm still expecting two of them. But we'll do this as part of the general amendment of the indictment we mentioned previously. All positive genetic reports have been disclosed to the Defence, and they either referred to someone who was named in a specific count of the indictment and then it was very easy to make the connection between the report and the indictment, or you were talking about someone who was not named in the indictment, and here they were covered by Counts 21 and 22, unidentified remains. In other words, the Defence has been informed gradually and at the same time as the Prosecution of the names of all persons covered by the indictment. Yes, it's true we've stated that we would give additional particulars about these -- the persons covered by Count 21 and 22. We'll do this as part of the amendment of the indictment as a whole, but the statements of the relatives or witnesses who could say something about the identified person, all this has been disclosed to the Defence and thus the Defence has been in a position to see what was the position in -- with respect to each identified persons. That's what we've been doing over the past few months. The Defence has in its possession exactly the same material, the same elements as the Prosecution, and all this is included in the statements of witness or relatives that we have already disclosed to the Defence. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having heard that, I would rather leave the issue there, and I take it the upcoming amendment will be the final one, and thereby we'll have the final indictment. Then I will turn to another issue, but I look at the clock. I'm not sure. Can I have a word with the court deputy, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we need to have a break. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was informed that we cannot go beyond half past 12.00, so we must bear that in mind. Now I turn to the issues of so-called exhumation materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I introduce that, and in doing so may I say that I'm confident, having had productive discussions between counsel on all sides during the adjournment that we will not come near to the 12.30 deadline, because most of the issues that are outstanding can be dealt with in relatively short order. As far as the exhumation position is concerned, there are 15 sets of remains which the Defence scientists have not yet had an opportunity to examine and whom the Defence would wish to have examined, and these are sets of remains that were returned or repatriated to the families of the alleged victims at a time prior to the point at which the Prosecution involved the Defence and granted access to remains before repatriation. The position at present is that those 15 sets of remains, subject to the obtaining of the appropriate consents, can be exhumed for further examination. As far as this year's concerned, probably up to and including the middle of December or thereabouts, but beyond that the winter conditions will set in and make exhumations impracticable. So time is to an extent of the essence. The Defence approached the relevant authorities within UNMIK for consents to have the exhumations conducted and for the necessary arrangements to be made. UNMIK's initial response was that this was a matter which should be directed to them as a request emanating from the Office of the Prosecutor, so the Defence turned to the Office of the Prosecutor who took the opposite view, namely that having completed their forensic examinations with those remains and having repatriated them, the Prosecution no longer has an interest in seeking their exhumation, and it's therefore a matter for liaison directly between the Defence and UNMIK. I should make it clear we have no objection at all to having the matter dealt with directly with UNMIK, but what we would need is a firm request from Your Honour to UNMIK to respond to a Defence request as they would respond to a Prosecution request, so that it becomes clear to UNMIK that requests for these exhumations do not need to be channeled through the Prosecution who do not wish to be the conduit for them. So that's the first point. The second point is that plainly the families's consents will need to be obtained, and under the arrangements governing all exhumations thus far it would be a Prosecution investigator who visited the families and obtained their consents. UNMIK does not undertake that responsibility. And so the consequence of the matter being dealt with in the way in which it is proposed that it should be dealt with is that the international elements of the Defence investigation team, that is to say the international investigators, would need to contact the relatives who -- whose consent is required and obtain their consent. Now, the Prosecution, as I understand it, have no objection to that course and neither do they have any objection to UNMIK responding directly to Defence requests to make the appropriate arrangements, nor, as I understand it, to Your Honour making that request, so to speak, formally on the record. So there is a practicable solution here, but it does need to have the imprint, if I can put it this way, of a court request, and it does need to have a clear mention on the record that the procedure would inevitably involve contact between Defence investigators and the relatives of the deceased. So that is the proposal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Involvement or confirmation of the Chamber is necessary for the contact with UNMIK, not with the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. What I'm inviting Your Honour to do is to confirm so that UNMIK can have the matter brought to their attention that it is appropriate for the Defence to make a request for exhumations directly to UNMIK and for UNMIK to process that request in exactly the same way as they would process a request from the Office of the Prosecutor. As far as the contact with families of deceased are concerned, I'm simply raising it on the public record so that the Prosecution are aware, and indeed they have been made aware independently of this, and so that all parties are aware before such a process were to begin that that would be the mechanism involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Any observation on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a number of bodies have been repatriated by the OMPF. The Defence has not had access to these remains. The Defence has had access to a number of remains but not to all of them. At some point we asked the OMPF to stop repatriating the remains for the Defence to have access to the other bodies. We do not oppose the Defence when it wishes to examine the remains and we do not oppose any request that the Defence might make to have access to these remains, but the Office of the Prosecutor believes that it does not need to involve itself in its operation. We've only taken note of the information provided to us by the Defence. We do not have any specific comments to make about this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would prefer to have a written motion in relation to that matter, to give some confirmation in the name of the Chamber to the UNMIK.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll undertake to do that very swiftly, but may I simply make the point again that to some extent time is of the essence because of the winter conditions making it impossible for exhumations to take place certainly beyond December and possibly at the back-end of December. So if we were to file the motion effectively within the next few days, might we, given that it's an unopposed motion, ask Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll bear that in mind, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. There are, in addition, two further matters raised under the exhumation heading. The first is the location of clothing which was originally found with certain of the recovered remains and photographed. The photographs have been disclosed to the Defence, but as Your Honour will see, our experts wish to examine the clothing itself, and we are in this respect entirely reliant on the Office of the Prosecutor to explain to us where and how the clothing items may be found. I mean, in a sense it's a corollary of Mr. Kelly's narrative examination of the forensic part of the case, because somewhere the clothing has become separated from the remains. Now, there have been certain items of clothing transmitted to The Hague, and some material has been made available for examination, but there is a significant quantity of clothing outstanding, and we are seeking the assistance of the Prosecution from its own involvement with these remains in tracing and identifying how and where the clothing can be made available for examination. And the final bullet point makes an analogous point in relation to bullets which were found at various points during the exhumations associated with or in certain sets of remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear the Prosecution's position. Yes. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall pick up on all these points in the right order. As far as the exhumation is concerned, the Prosecution would rather have the international experts deal with this and not ask whether these people are witnesses for the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, as far as the clothing are concerned and other exhibits are concerned. As far as the clothing are concerned, to begin with, for those bodies which were already repatriated in 2003, the feeling I have is the clothing was handed back to the families as well as the bodies. As far as those bodies which have not been repatriated are concerned and which the Defence have access to, the clothing was made available in the morgue of the OMPF in Pristina, and the Defence was able to access these in order to examine them. When we repatriated a number of bodies after the Defence had examined the body in Pristina, we quite clearly asked the Defence whether they would accept that the clothing be handed over to the families at the same time as the bodies, and the Defence at the time did not object to this. So all the clothing which the Defence wishes to examine now, all these clothing are in the hands of the OMPF, clothing which they have had access to when the body was in the morgue in 2006. As for as various items are concerned, exhibit, bullet fragments and other things found during the exhumations, the Office of the Prosecutor has received a set of data. These data were disclosed to the Defence in writing a few months ago, and more recently after the Defence had occasion to look at the bodies in the morgue in Pristina, the OTP indicated that they had further data and asked the UNMIK to seize all the remaining items and hand them over to the OTP. This was indeed done. This was at the end of the August, beginning of September. In a mail addressed to the Defence, I would like to draw the attention here, Mr. Haradinaj's Defence counsel in particular, we have received a new set of exhibits, and I think he wishes to go there around the 19th or 20th of September. Bullet traces, et cetera, were included in an application sent to the UNMIK. The latter have been received by the OTP and handed over to the Defence. Now, if certain items need to be addressed in greater detail, perhaps we can discuss this with Defence counsel. After the hearing, we can compare the documents and take stock of the situation with them, if they so wish. I think if we go into the detail of all of this now we will not be able to finish off on time because our time is limited. As far as I can understand, I think the Defence has been able to access everything that has been made available to us, and maybe we could discuss this after the hearing, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for the clarification, and there was some additional information in what Mr. Dutertre has just said. May I endorse his suggestion that rather than take up Your Honour's time with the detail of this, in the spirit of cooperation arrangements might be discussed between the parties to see if we can progress the identification of those missing fragments and ascertain their location, in which case there's nothing further that I need to trouble Your Honour with under the heading of exhumations. Can I deal briefly and in turn with the position as far as other items of disclosure are concerned? May I pass over the first one and come back to it in just a moment because it is, I think, the only one that remains substantially in contention for the purposes of today's hearing. The second bullet point asks for clarification of certain information which was disclosed to the Defence in an incomplete and redacted form, and there's been some extended correspondence between the parties about it. Having discussed the matter with my learned friends over the adjournment, the proposal is that by the 24th, the same date that Your Honour has specified thus far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: 25th, I'm sorry, in respect of other procedural steps, the Prosecution will notify the Defence of the best information that they have in respect of the request that that bullet refers to. The same proposal is made in respect of the following bullet point, which is the source of a public denial by Witness SST7/14 of certain allegations that are made by the Prosecution. The public denial was referred to in an OTP pleading on protective measures, and we have been requesting for some time the source and any record of that public denial, and again that is a matter which the Prosecution have indicated that they will look into and respond to by the 25th. There is nothing that the Defence would wish to raise at this stage in relation to search criteria, save that the Prosecution and the Defence are agreed, as I understand the position, that the Prosecution will provide the Defence with the results of its searches and that as and when and the Defence makes specific requests and invite the Prosecution to run them, then the Prosecution will respond with appropriate expedition to those requests as and when received, and there's nothing further we need to trouble Your Honour with in that respect either. As far as the last bullet point is concerned, it is a request made effectively yesterday for confirmation as to whether or not the Prosecution had taken a statement from a named individual -- or I'm sorry, from two named individuals. The position has been clarified in respect of the first. There is no statement from that witness. As far as the second is concerned, again the Prosecution will provide the Defence with an answer by the 25th. That leaves the first bullet point which remains a matter of contention, and may I outline it very briefly. Witness SST7/30 is a witness of some importance to the Prosecution's case against Mr. Haradinaj and a witness whose credibility inevitably is in issue in these proceedings. The Prosecution have disclosed to the Defence an investigator's letter under the reference number that there appears indicating that a source had informed the Prosecution that somebody who is referred to as the agent had been told by Witness SST7/30 that he was willing to withdraw his testimony against Mr. Haradinaj in return for the payment of 5 million euros. In other words, it is an offer by the witness as reported in effect to change his position if a bribe were offered to him. And that's obviously a matter which is highly relevant to that witness's credibility, and we seek to explore it through the source by which this information came to the Prosecution. As matters currently stand as we understand it, the Prosecution does not have the particulars of the agent who was the immediate recipient of that information but does have the particulars of the source. And again I'll allow the Prosecution to clarify their position in just a moment, but as I understand it, the Prosecution take the view that that source should now have an effective veto over whether the Defence should be provided with the mechanisms for investigating this because he's not prepared to have -- he or she is not prepared to have his identification disclosed to the Defence so that the matter can be properly and thoroughly investigated. We of course persist in our request that the unredacted material, including the identification of the source of that information be disclosed to the Defence, so that this highly relevant inquiry can be properly pursued. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honour pleases, Mr. Emmerson has fairly clearly set out the position. The letter was in fact a redacted letter. They -- the Defence were in fact seeking the full disclosure of the full letter. The Prosecution has made clear that it will not disclose that particular document. It's an internal work product, and we're not obliged to disclose it and will not do so. Mr. Emmerson accurately informed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It's a work letter. It's an internal work product. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's an investigator's letter, a report or letter -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, it's an internal memo, if Your Honour please. It's internal material so we're not going to disclose that. I don't know that the Defence are necessarily pursuing that. What I think they're more interested in is the information. Insofar as the agent, the personality referred to as the agent is concerned, the Prosecution doesn't have any details as to his identity or contact information for that person.
